segment.text: 男も女も、その顔にはまだ少しの皺もよってなかった。しかし男の濃い眉毛の陰のくぼんだ優しさうな瞳には、だるさうな疲れの色が見えてゐた。そして女の濃い髪のいろや、細やかな肩のあたりには、なほ打沈んだやうな深い疲れと、まどろむやうな安らかさとが見えてゐた。

segment.text: 彼女は鍋から熱い炊き立ての、白い湯気が一ぱい立ち上ってる御飯をついで彼に渡した。そして彼女の若い大きな瞳も、母親らしい嬉しさにみちて子供の瞬間もぢっとしてない、小鳥のやうに愛らしい様子を見つめた。そして、たまらなささうに、この子はどうしたといふんだらう、とふと口の中に独言を云ひながら、どうにも仕方がない程可愛いといふやうな様子で、『坊や、』と強く云ったけれども、笑が顔からあふれて了って、彼女は助をかりるやうに男の顔を見た。そして三人は、すべての事を忘れてしまった様に、子供の為めに互にどうしようかといふ様に笑ひ合った。そして子供の為めに、彼等は暖かい賑かさと、其上に自然に溢れる笑ひと嬉しさを持って食事にとりかゝったのであった。また彼等は、ごた〳〵した騒がしさの為に、雨風の音を耳にしない。

head.reason: Both name the same crux: bad potato taste opening interior time where suffering seen from far end becomes nostalgia and forgiveness, served by repetition and non-resolution. Option 0 states it more fully, adding the three-year shock, change of tense rather than consolation, and husband's non-understanding with smaller practical resolve.
head.say: Both cruxes name the same temporal slippage; proceeding on first read.

crux.for_the_english: Keep the potato dull, not vivid: hard, crackly, cold, tasteless. Do not enliven it, moralize it, or explain the association. Let the long, slow, almost unmoving sentences of p12-p17 stand against the noisy, crowded supper sentences of p5-p9, and do not tidy the tense drift, subject-dropping, or repetition.
crux.point: The whole story turns on a sensory failure that opens into interior time: one mouthful of badly cooked potato stops the warm noisy supper and sends the young mother into a prolonged still vision.
crux.why: p1-p9 build noise, crowding, laughter and mutual looking at the child; p10-p11 break it with a single taste — potato frozen-hard, dry, tasteless. From there to p18 almost nothing outward happens while she remembers three years of poverty, sickness, fear and then sees a dim picture of three quiet people telling a never-ending story in which all good and evil become nostalgia and forgiveness. If that passage is read as flashback, reverie, or social comment, the architecture collapses.

crux.for_the_english: Fix single English equivalents for yasurakasa, sabishii/samishii, natsukashimi, yurushi, and reuse them even where English wants synonyms; preserve the paradoxes lonely-peaceful, sad-nostalgic, and never identify the three people in the vision.
crux.point: The vision only works by deliberate repetition and refusal to resolve, ending where it began with the storm.
crux.why: The same words circle from p4 night's yasurakasa, through p12-p13 distant lonely heart and suffering-become-nostalgic-dream, to p16-p17 all things becoming natsukashimi to yurushi before night-like rest, to p20 and p34-35. The three figures are never named — family grown old, dead, Trinity, no one — and the final 'Arashi da na' repeats p1 but now heard in stillness. Clarifying who they are or varying the key nouns for elegance rewrites the ending into hopefulness the text does not grant.

second.say: A young family eats noisily in a storm while the baby bangs its spoon. The mother tastes a cold tasteless potato and falls inward: three years of married poverty feel suddenly long, old, dream-like. She sees three still people telling an endless story where everything becomes nostalgia and forgiveness before night-like rest. She returns with only 'only three years' and quiet resolve to work, nurse, sleep, while the storm remains outside.
second.what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence from letters, drafts, or contemporary reception that the three figures are a specific dated allegory or that 'Supper' was read as straightforward proletarian optimism would make me drop the ambiguity crux.

crux.for_the_english: Keep the syntax drifting where hers drifts: the long, additive sentences, the repeated returns to the same few words — far, quiet, smile, tiredness, dream, nostalgia (懐かしみ), forgiveness (許し), peace/rest (安らかさ) — and do not vary them for elegance. Keep the vision grammatically and referentially unfixed: we are not told who the three are, where they are, or whether this is old age, death, or a picture in her eyes. In particular, do not turn あの日 / その日 into 'heaven', 'when we die', or 'someday when things get better'. The husband must not be made to understand what he has not understood; the closing resolve to work, clear up, and get up early must stay deliberately smaller and more practical than her vision.
crux.point: The crux is time seen from its far end. A mouthful of badly cooked potato — cold, hard, gritty, tasteless in the middle of an otherwise warm supper — suddenly detaches the young mother from the present, and she sees her marriage's poverty, fear, illness, and exhaustion as if from a vast distance after it has all passed, when suffering will have become 'nostalgia and forgiveness'. The shock the text keeps returning to is measurable and must not be softened: only three years have passed (p14, p22–27), yet inside the life it feels interminable and she feels already old (p13). Her vision (p16–17) is not a plan or an escape fantasy so much as a change of tense: the present, looked at as already past and forgiven, becomes bearable, and she can come back to the table, smile, and agree to keep working (p20, p34–35). A translation that explains this — as a daydream, a premonition of death, religious consolation, or marital hopefulness — will make it smaller and clearer than it is.
crux.why: Everything structural serves that slippage. The story barely moves: a storm outside, a crowded table cleared so the baby cannot grab things, a meal begun, a potato tasted, a husband twice asking why she is silent, a brief exchange counting the years, the child fed and put to the breast, the table to be cleared. Against that stillness the interior passages lengthen and loosen, subjects drop away, and 'she remembered / she was seeing' shades into a picture that is at once in her eyes, in the future, and in a dim light with three quiet figures telling an endless story that contains all good and evil, grief, anger, and joy while no one moves and everyone smiles (p16). The comfort is inseparable from its strangeness: what consoles her is not that suffering will stop soon — the dialogue at the end admits it will not — but that from far enough away it will no longer need to be answered.

open_questions.question: Are the three figures in the vision the family grown old, the family after death, or an deliberately unidentifiable trio? The text gives three people, bowed heads, nostalgia and forgiveness as if before an eternal, night-like rest — suggestive of age and death but never naming either. The editor needs to rule how much, if at all, the English may lean toward the funereal; my reading is to lean not at all.
open_questions.why_it_matters: If the figures become 'themselves as an old couple' or 'in the afterlife', the vision hardens into doctrine and the final return to work loses its odd, unresolved consolation.

open_questions.question: The baby is explicitly a girl (女の子, p2; 彼女, p7), yet both parents address her as 坊や, literally 'little boy' but usable as a fond generic for a baby. Render as 'baby', a name-like 'little one', or keep 'boy' with the contradiction visible?
open_questions.why_it_matters: 'Boy' in English will read as an authorial error or a bible inconsistency; 'baby' loses the period, colloquial warmth of the address and the way it punctuates the parents' delight at p8, p29–30.

open_questions.question: How eschatological is あの日 / 安息? 安息 can be ordinary rest or eternal rest. Is her 'day when everything changes into nostalgia and forgiveness' a day in this life (old age looking back), the approach of death, or intentionally both?
open_questions.why_it_matters: This governs single words at the story's summit — 'rest', 'repose', 'peace', 'that day' — and whether the ending reads as endurance within life or as quietly longing for its end.

body.reading:
Begin with the frame, because the translation must be able to come back to it: the story opens on the storm as a bare perception ('Outside the now-dark door, a violent sound of rain and wind — a storm', p1) and ends with the husband stopped still, whispering the same fact ('It's a storm', p38). In between, the family is for a while too noisy and absorbed to hear it at all (p8), and the wife hears it again, quietly, at exactly the moment she re-enters her vision after her husband's first question (p19). The storm is not a symbol to be underlined; it is the outside world and the passing of the evening, first unnoticed, then registered from inside her distance. Keep its three appearances plain and verbally linked, and keep the final line bare and unadorned — nothing has been solved, the child is simply asleep at the breast and the room has gone quiet.

The opening supper needs its full physical warmth and disorder, because the vision only detaches from something solid. The parents are young and unwrinkled but already worn (p3): tiredness in his hollowed, gentle eyes, a deeper tiredness and a sleepy peace about her hair and shoulders. Their tenderness is enacted, not stated — everything grabbable moved under the table, the baby drumming spoon and plate, the father's whole face breaking into a smile he tries to contain while he feeds her and crams rice into his own mouth in the gaps, the parents laughing at each other over the child (p5–10). Do not ennoble this into glowing poverty or cuteness, and do not flatten it either: the baby's chubby roundness, long lashes, quick clever hands, the big red hand, the steam off the rice, the deep blue pot of beef and onion, carrot and potato, are the counterweight. If this half is thinned, her stillness at the potato will look like the story's default mood rather than a fall out of shared life.

The potato itself (p10–12) must stay oddly literal. It is not merely disappointing: bitten expecting it sweet and soft, it is as if frozen, hard and gritty (ざくざく), profoundly tasteless, and she re-bites it with her front teeth in surprise. The text insists on the tastelessness as 無味, unrelated (かかはりのない) and cold, and it is that unrelated quality that gives her 'a quiet, lonely, far-away heart'. Resist making the potato 'symbolise' her marriage in the English; the Japanese lets a contingent, almost accidental sensation open the distance, and the slight disproportion is the point. Likewise keep the sequence of her remembering unsorted — days of tears, days threatened and frightened over material things, days of illness, all already dreamlike and even the suffering nostalgic while she remembers it (p13) — rather than rationalising it into a summary of three hard years.

Her register is the story's main technical risk. Shizu's prose in the interior sections is repetitive, incantatory and syntactically loose, circling: ながい物語り 'a long story told without ceasing', then ながい生活、ながい悲しみ、ながい苦しみ in p20; 静か, 遠い, なつかしみ, 許し, 安らかさ recurring as a small chord rather than a developing argument. Berman's usual deformations are all waiting here: clarification (naming the three figures, explaining the day), expansion (adding connective reasoning between the potato, the memory, the vision and the smile), ennoblement (lifting her plain vision into lyrical transcendence), and destroying the network of repetitions by elegantly varying 'long', 'quiet', 'far' and 'smile'. The couple's dialogue offers some protection and must keep its own plainness and slight non-sequitur: 'Why are you so quiet?' — 'It really has been only a little while, hasn't it, since we married' (p21–22). She is not answering his question; she is bringing the vision's arithmetic back into the room. His answering count — just three years, and yet we've suffered; in a while the baby will walk (p25, p28) — is fond, practical, and knowingly inadequate. Do not harmonise the two registers into one shared understanding. The story ends not in communion about the vision, which he never hears, but in parallel resolve: his 'It won't be much longer' (もう少しの間だ, p34) spoken almost to himself, her calm 'Then let us work' (p35), clearing up and early rising tomorrow (p36). Her hope, if that is the word, is private, disproportionate, and returns as housework and sleep.

A few smaller things the translator should watch. The child is a baby girl who can just stand holding the table, yet the parents call her 坊や; see the open questions rather than silently fixing it. The marriage's three years are stated three times in different keys (narrated at p14, marvelled at by her at p22 and p27, confirmed by him at p25); keep all three, since the repetition is the measure of the distortion. The vision's story-within is told by and to the three figures across what seems a lifetime; avoid past-tense summary that makes it safely concluded — it is still going on, no one moves, the smile continues (p16). Finally, watch the smiles: the word 微笑/笑み belongs to the laughing parents at the table, to the unmoving figures in the vision, and to the wife alone as she comes back from it (p20) and turns to her husband 'as if with nostalgia' (p21). Varying or dropping it where it recurs will break the thin thread by which the supper and the vision are, quietly, the same scene seen at two distances.
body.say: I can read the broad movement with confidence, but I cannot settle from the text alone whether the vision in p16–18 is meant as old age, death, or a deliberately timeless elsewhere; nor whether 坊や for a baby explicitly called a girl is ordinary period usage or a marked choice. I have flagged both rather than resolving them in the reading.

payload.say: I can read the broad movement with confidence, but I cannot settle from the text alone whether the vision in p16–18 is meant as old age, death, or a deliberately timeless elsewhere; nor whether 坊や for a baby explicitly called a girl is ordinary period usage or a marked choice. I have flagged both rather than resolving them in the reading.

crux.for_the_english: Keep the syntax drifting where hers drifts: the long, additive sentences, the repeated returns to the same few words — far, quiet, smile, tiredness, dream, nostalgia (懐かしみ), forgiveness (許し), peace/rest (安らかさ) — and do not vary them for elegance. Keep the vision grammatically and referentially unfixed: we are not told who the three are, where they are, or whether this is old age, death, or a picture in her eyes. In particular, do not turn あの日 / その日 into 'heaven', 'when we die', or 'someday when things get better'. The husband must not be made to understand what he has not understood; the closing resolve to work, clear up, and get up early must stay deliberately smaller and more practical than her vision.
crux.point: The crux is time seen from its far end. A mouthful of badly cooked potato — cold, hard, gritty, tasteless in the middle of an otherwise warm supper — suddenly detaches the young mother from the present, and she sees her marriage's poverty, fear, illness, and exhaustion as if from a vast distance after it has all passed, when suffering will have become 'nostalgia and forgiveness'. The shock the text keeps returning to is measurable and must not be softened: only three years have passed (p14, p22–27), yet inside the life it feels interminable and she feels already old (p13). Her vision (p16–17) is not a plan or an escape fantasy so much as a change of tense: the present, looked at as already past and forgiven, becomes bearable, and she can come back to the table, smile, and agree to keep working (p20, p34–35). A translation that explains this — as a daydream, a premonition of death, religious consolation, or marital hopefulness — will make it smaller and clearer than it is.
crux.why: Everything structural serves that slippage. The story barely moves: a storm outside, a crowded table cleared so the baby cannot grab things, a meal begun, a potato tasted, a husband twice asking why she is silent, a brief exchange counting the years, the child fed and put to the breast, the table to be cleared. Against that stillness the interior passages lengthen and loosen, subjects drop away, and 'she remembered / she was seeing' shades into a picture that is at once in her eyes, in the future, and in a dim light with three quiet figures telling an endless story that contains all good and evil, grief, anger, and joy while no one moves and everyone smiles (p16). The comfort is inseparable from its strangeness: what consoles her is not that suffering will stop soon — the dialogue at the end admits it will not — but that from far enough away it will no longer need to be answered.

payload.say: A young family eats noisily in a storm while the baby bangs its spoon. She returns with only 'only three years' and quiet resolve to work, nurse, sleep, while the storm remains outside.

crux.for_the_english: Keep the potato dull, not vivid: hard, crackly, cold, tasteless. Do not enliven it, moralize it, or explain the association. Let the long, slow, almost unmoving sentences of p12-p17 stand against the noisy, crowded supper sentences of p5-p9, and do not tidy the tense drift, subject-dropping, or repetition.
crux.point: The whole story turns on a sensory failure that opens into interior time: one mouthful of badly cooked potato stops the warm noisy supper and sends the young mother into a prolonged still vision.
crux.why: p1-p9 build noise, crowding, laughter and mutual looking at the child; p10-p11 break it with a single taste — potato frozen-hard, dry, tasteless. From there to p18 almost nothing outward happens while she remembers three years of poverty, sickness, fear and then sees a dim picture of three quiet people telling a never-ending story in which all good and evil become nostalgia and forgiveness. If that passage is read as flashback, reverie, or social comment, the architecture collapses.

crux.for_the_english: Fix single English equivalents for yasurakasa, sabishii/samishii, natsukashimi, yurushi, and reuse them even where English wants synonyms; preserve the paradoxes lonely-peaceful, sad-nostalgic, and never identify the three people in the vision.
crux.point: The vision only works by deliberate repetition and refusal to resolve, ending where it began with the storm.
crux.why: The same words circle from p4 night's yasurakasa, through p12-p13 distant lonely heart and suffering-become-nostalgic-dream, to p16-p17 all things becoming natsukashimi to yurushi before night-like rest, to p20 and p34-35. The three figures are never named — family grown old, dead, Trinity, no one — and the final 'Arashi da na' repeats p1 but now heard in stillness. Clarifying who they are or varying the key nouns for elegance rewrites the ending into hopefulness the text does not grant.

crux.for_the_english: Keep the syntax drifting where hers drifts: the long, additive sentences, the repeated returns to the same few words — far, quiet, smile, tiredness, dream, nostalgia (懐かしみ), forgiveness (許し), peace/rest (安らかさ) — and do not vary them for elegance. Keep the vision grammatically and referentially unfixed: we are not told who the three are, where they are, or whether this is old age, death, or a picture in her eyes. In particular, do not turn あの日 / その日 into 'heaven', 'when we die', or 'someday when things get better'. The husband must not be made to understand what he has not understood; the closing resolve to work, clear up, and get up early must stay deliberately smaller and more practical than her vision.
crux.point: The crux is time seen from its far end. A mouthful of badly cooked potato — cold, hard, gritty, tasteless in the middle of an otherwise warm supper — suddenly detaches the young mother from the present, and she sees her marriage's poverty, fear, illness, and exhaustion as if from a vast distance after it has all passed, when suffering will have become 'nostalgia and forgiveness'. The shock the text keeps returning to is measurable and must not be softened: only three years have passed (p14, p22–27), yet inside the life it feels interminable and she feels already old (p13). Her vision (p16–17) is not a plan or an escape fantasy so much as a change of tense: the present, looked at as already past and forgiven, becomes bearable, and she can come back to the table, smile, and agree to keep working (p20, p34–35). A translation that explains this — as a daydream, a premonition of death, religious consolation, or marital hopefulness — will make it smaller and clearer than it is.
crux.why: Everything structural serves that slippage. The story barely moves: a storm outside, a crowded table cleared so the baby cannot grab things, a meal begun, a potato tasted, a husband twice asking why she is silent, a brief exchange counting the years, the child fed and put to the breast, the table to be cleared. Against that stillness the interior passages lengthen and loosen, subjects drop away, and 'she remembered / she was seeing' shades into a picture that is at once in her eyes, in the future, and in a dim light with three quiet figures telling an endless story that contains all good and evil, grief, anger, and joy while no one moves and everyone smiles (p16). The comfort is inseparable from its strangeness: what consoles her is not that suffering will stop soon — the dialogue at the end admits it will not — but that from far enough away it will no longer need to be answered.

open_questions.question: Are the three figures in the vision the family grown old, the family after death, or an deliberately unidentifiable trio? The text gives three people, bowed heads, nostalgia and forgiveness as if before an eternal, night-like rest — suggestive of age and death but never naming either. The editor needs to rule how much, if at all, the English may lean toward the funereal; my reading is to lean not at all.
open_questions.why_it_matters: If the figures become 'themselves as an old couple' or 'in the afterlife', the vision hardens into doctrine and the final return to work loses its odd, unresolved consolation.

open_questions.question: The baby is explicitly a girl (女の子, p2; 彼女, p7), yet both parents address her as 坊や, literally 'little boy' but usable as a fond generic for a baby. Render as 'baby', a name-like 'little one', or keep 'boy' with the contradiction visible?
open_questions.why_it_matters: 'Boy' in English will read as an authorial error or a bible inconsistency; 'baby' loses the period, colloquial warmth of the address and the way it punctuates the parents' delight at p8, p29–30.

open_questions.question: How eschatological is あの日 / 安息? 安息 can be ordinary rest or eternal rest. Is her 'day when everything changes into nostalgia and forgiveness' a day in this life (old age looking back), the approach of death, or intentionally both?
open_questions.why_it_matters: This governs single words at the story's summit — 'rest', 'repose', 'peace', 'that day' — and whether the ending reads as endurance within life or as quietly longing for its end.

reading.reading:
Begin with the frame, because the translation must be able to come back to it: the story opens on the storm as a bare perception ('Outside the now-dark door, a violent sound of rain and wind — a storm', p1) and ends with the husband stopped still, whispering the same fact ('It's a storm', p38). In between, the family is for a while too noisy and absorbed to hear it at all (p8), and the wife hears it again, quietly, at exactly the moment she re-enters her vision after her husband's first question (p19). The storm is not a symbol to be underlined; it is the outside world and the passing of the evening, first unnoticed, then registered from inside her distance. Keep its three appearances plain and verbally linked, and keep the final line bare and unadorned — nothing has been solved, the child is simply asleep at the breast and the room has gone quiet.

The opening supper needs its full physical warmth and disorder, because the vision only detaches from something solid. The parents are young and unwrinkled but already worn (p3): tiredness in his hollowed, gentle eyes, a deeper tiredness and a sleepy peace about her hair and shoulders. Their tenderness is enacted, not stated — everything grabbable moved under the table, the baby drumming spoon and plate, the father's whole face breaking into a smile he tries to contain while he feeds her and crams rice into his own mouth in the gaps, the parents laughing at each other over the child (p5–10). Do not ennoble this into glowing poverty or cuteness, and do not flatten it either: the baby's chubby roundness, long lashes, quick clever hands, the big red hand, the steam off the rice, the deep blue pot of beef and onion, carrot and potato, are the counterweight. If this half is thinned, her stillness at the potato will look like the story's default mood rather than a fall out of shared life.

The potato itself (p10–12) must stay oddly literal. It is not merely disappointing: bitten expecting it sweet and soft, it is as if frozen, hard and gritty (ざくざく), profoundly tasteless, and she re-bites it with her front teeth in surprise. The text insists on the tastelessness as 無味, unrelated (かかはりのない) and cold, and it is that unrelated quality that gives her 'a quiet, lonely, far-away heart'. Resist making the potato 'symbolise' her marriage in the English; the Japanese lets a contingent, almost accidental sensation open the distance, and the slight disproportion is the point. Likewise keep the sequence of her remembering unsorted — days of tears, days threatened and frightened over material things, days of illness, all already dreamlike and even the suffering nostalgic while she remembers it (p13) — rather than rationalising it into a summary of three hard years.

Her register is the story's main technical risk. Shizu's prose in the interior sections is repetitive, incantatory and syntactically loose, circling: ながい物語り 'a long story told without ceasing', then ながい生活、ながい悲しみ、ながい苦しみ in p20; 静か, 遠い, なつかしみ, 許し, 安らかさ recurring as a small chord rather than a developing argument. Berman's usual deformations are all waiting here: clarification (naming the three figures, explaining the day), expansion (adding connective reasoning between the potato, the memory, the vision and the smile), ennoblement (lifting her plain vision into lyrical transcendence), and destroying the network of repetitions by elegantly varying 'long', 'quiet', 'far' and 'smile'. The couple's dialogue offers some protection and must keep its own plainness and slight non-sequitur: 'Why are you so quiet?' — 'It really has been only a little while, hasn't it, since we married' (p21–22). She is not answering his question; she is bringing the vision's arithmetic back into the room. His answering count — just three years, and yet we've suffered; in a while the baby will walk (p25, p28) — is fond, practical, and knowingly inadequate. Do not harmonise the two registers into one shared understanding. The story ends not in communion about the vision, which he never hears, but in parallel resolve: his 'It won't be much longer' (もう少しの間だ, p34) spoken almost to himself, her calm 'Then let us work' (p35), clearing up and early rising tomorrow (p36). Her hope, if that is the word, is private, disproportionate, and returns as housework and sleep.

A few smaller things the translator should watch. The child is a baby girl who can just stand holding the table, yet the parents call her 坊や; see the open questions rather than silently fixing it. The marriage's three years are stated three times in different keys (narrated at p14, marvelled at by her at p22 and p27, confirmed by him at p25); keep all three, since the repetition is the measure of the distortion. The vision's story-within is told by and to the three figures across what seems a lifetime; avoid past-tense summary that makes it safely concluded — it is still going on, no one moves, the smile continues (p16). Finally, watch the smiles: the word 微笑/笑み belongs to the laughing parents at the table, to the unmoving figures in the vision, and to the wife alone as she comes back from it (p20) and turns to her husband 'as if with nostalgia' (p21). Varying or dropping it where it recurs will break the thin thread by which the supper and the vision are, quietly, the same scene seen at two distances.
reading.say: I can read the broad movement with confidence, but I cannot settle from the text alone whether the vision in p16–18 is meant as old age, death, or a deliberately timeless elsewhere; nor whether 坊や for a baby explicitly called a girl is ordinary period usage or a marked choice. I have flagged both rather than resolving them in the reading.

And as if she could not bear it, muttering to herself, 'Whatever is to be done with this child,' as if the child were dear beyond all managing, she said firmly, "“Bōya” as parental call — proposed: keep as “little one / baby” with note, not “little boy”," but a smile overflowed from her face, and she looked at the man's face as if asking for help. And the three, as if they had forgotten everything, smiled at each other over the child, as if wondering what to do for the child. And for the child, they set about the meal with a warm bustle, and with a smile and gladness welling up of itself on top of it. And with the clattering noise, they did not hear the sound of rain and wind.

curious.ja: 若い父親は、彼の赤く大きな片手を忙しくテーブルの上に拡げてゐた。そしてその眼は子供によって仕方がなく湧き出た笑を堪へながら、子供をさゝへて、その小さな赤い口に僅の食物を入れてやった。そのすきに彼は、あわたゞしく大きな口を開けた、彼は彼自身の口のなかに御飯を押し込んだ。

curious.en: The mother, leaning against the wall, bowed and silent, heaped onto a white plate the beef and onion, the carrot and beef, onion, carrot and potato [jagaimo] simmered sweet-soft simmered in the deep blue pot. And about to say something, she put a beef, onion, carrot and potato [jagaimo] simmered sweet-soft simmered sweet and soft into her mouth and looked at the man's face, but as if noticing something, she suddenly shut her mouth and gazed blankly at a far place.
curious.ja: 母親は、壁によって黙ってうつむきながら藍色の深い鍋に煮た牛肉と玉葱と、人参とジャガ芋とを白い皿に盛ってゐた。そしてなにか云はうとして、甘く柔かく煮たジャガ芋を口のなかに入れて、男の顔を見たが、彼女はなにかに気がついたやうに、ふと口を閉ぢて茫然と遠い所を見た。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: The beef, onion, carrot and potato [jagaimo] simmered sweet-soft in her mouth was hard as if frozen, gritty and crunching, and very bad-tasting. Silently, as if startled, she re-bit it with her front teeth, but her heart had already bowed down, lonely.
curious.ja: 彼女の口のなかのジャガ芋が、丁度凍ったかのやうに固くざく〳〵してゐて、非常に不味かったのだった。彼女はふと驚いたやうに黙って前歯でかみなほしたが、彼女の心は、いつか淋しくうつむいてしまってゐた。
curious.label: house-checked

notes.body: The potato is jagaimo in a sweet-soft simmered stew; zaku-zaku names its gritty, crunching hardness when badly cooked. The translation keeps the small, literal disappointment that gives her distance.

curious.en: She had remembered the suffering and grief and tiredness of each day. And the tasteless, unrelated, cold badness of the beef, onion, carrot and potato [jagaimo] simmered sweet-soft gave her a quiet, lonely, far-away heart. She pictured the poor, grief-filled real life after marriage.
curious.ja: 彼女は日々の苦しみや悲しみ疲れを思出したのであった。そしてジャガ芋の無味な、かゝはりのない冷やかな不味さが、彼女に静かな淋しい遠くはなれた心を与へた。彼女は結婚後の貧しい悲しみにみちた現実の生活を思ひ浮べたのであった。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: And it seemed like a life dragged on far too long. She felt suddenly as if she herself had grown quite old. And quietly, with a far heart, she was quietly remembering the tear-filled days, and the days spent threatened and afraid over material things, and the days, day by day, grieved and suffered through illness. But to her remembering now, everything was like a dream. Suffering too, grief too, were like a nostalgic dream.
curious.ja: そして、それがあまりに永く引きつゞいた生活のやうにも思はれた。彼女はふと自分がすっかり老いてしまったかのやうに考へられた。そして静かに涙にみちた日のことや、物質の為めに脅かされ恐れてすごした日々や、病の為めに悲しみ苦しんだその日その日のことを遠い心が静かに思出してゐるのだった。けれどもいま思出してる彼女には、すべてが夢のやうであった。苦しみも悲しみもなつかしい夢のやうであった。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: And when you think about it, it was only about three years of life since marriage.
curious.ja: そして考へて見れば、わづかに結婚後の三年ばかりの生活にすぎない。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: Before she knew it, as if caught by something, she gazed blankly toward the far distance. Her quiet heart was already seeing something like a phantom picture.
curious.ja: 彼女は、いつとなく何物にか気をとられたやうに、ぼんやりと遠くの方を見てゐた。彼女のその静かな心が、いつか幻のやうな絵を見てゐたのであった。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: It was in a dim light, and, quiet like that light, three people drawing close with heads together, telling a long story. The story seemed to go on and on between them, for so long without ever breaking off. And in that story, all the good and evil of the world, sadness and suffering and anger and anguish and joy, everything seemed to be told. But teller and listener only quietly, peacefully, went on smiling, and they did not move at all. With heads bent and eyes lowered, only a quiet nostalgia and forgiveness seemed to wrap them there. And there too a deep, deep peace showed over all of them.
curious.ja: それは淡暗い光りのなかに、そしてその光りのやうに物静かな三人の人たちが、より合って頭をあつめてながい物語りをしてゐるのだった。その物語りは、あまりにながく絶えることなく彼等の間につゞけられてゐるやうであった。そしてその物語りのなかには、すべて世の中の善や悪や、かなしみや苦しみ怒りもなやみも、よろこびもすべてが語られてるやうだった。けれども話す人も聞く人も、たゞ静かに安らかにぢっと微笑をつゞけてゐるばかりであって、彼等は少しも動かなかった。首をかたむけて眼を伏せながら、そして、そこにはたゞ静かななつかしみと、許しとが彼等をつつんでゐるやうに見えた。そしてまたそこには深い〳〵安らかさが彼等のすべてに表はれてゐるのであった。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: All the things of the world, a life, will pass. And on that day [ano hi] when it has passed, everything, all things, will for the first time change into nostalgia and forgiveness. And at that day [ano hi] they are before an eternal rest [ansoku] / peace [yasurakasa] like night.
curious.ja: 世の中の總ての事、人生は過去るであらう。そして過去った其日に初めて總てが、總ての事が懐しみと許しとに変る事だらう。そして其時彼等は永久に夜の様な安息の前にあるのであった。
curious.label: house-checked

notes.body: Japanese uses two different words where English has peace: yasurakasa for a calm peacefulness, and here ansoku for rest, which can mean ordinary rest or a last rest. The story leaves it plain and does not name heaven or death.

curious.en: The far picture was reflected dark and quiet in the bottom of her eyes. And through the bottom of her eyes, far off into the future, with a lonely peace, that picture could be seen. Young, alone, she gave a lonely secret sigh, and, glancing at the scattered table and the faces of her husband and child, she stayed silent.
curious.ja: 遠い絵が暗く静かに、彼女の眼の底に映ってゐた。また瞳の底を通して遠く未来に、淋しい安らかさを持って、その絵が見えるのであった。若い彼女は一人で淋しいひそかな溜息をついた、そして、とり散らされたテーブルの上と、夫と子供の顔をちらと見ながら黙ってゐた。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "Why are you so quiet?" The man looked at the woman's face in sudden wonder and spoke to her. She hurried to say something, but unable to say it all at once she fell silent, and again her eyes ran far away. And she saw the phantom picture again. Then for the first time she quietly heard the sound of the storm [aramashi — arashi] outside the door. She said nothing.
curious.ja: 『どうして黙ってるの。』男は、ふと不思議さうに女の顔を見て声をかけた。彼女は、あわてゝなにかを云はうとしたが、一口には何事も云ひかねて黙ってしまふと、再びその眼が遠く走ってしまった。そして彼女は、また幻の絵を見たのだった。彼女は、その時はじめて戸の外の嵐の音を、静かに耳にした。彼女はなにも云はずにゐた。
curious.label: house-checked

notes.body: The storm opened the story and was then forgotten in the table noise; here she hears it again, quietly, from inside her distance.
notes.span: Then for the first time she quietly heard the sound of the {t:storm} outside the door.

curious.en: Yes. There is that day [ano hi]. There is that day [ano hi] when everything changes into nostalgia and forgiveness and rest [ansoku] / peace [yasurakasa]. After a long life, and after a long grief, and after a long suffering, on the day after that, there is that peaceful that day [ano hi] of nostalgia and forgiveness. What is the suffering and grief of each single day. What is the tiredness and worry of each single day. Before she knew it she was smiling a smile.
curious.ja: さうだ。あの日があるのだ。あのすべてがなつかしみと許しと、安らかさに変る日があるのだった。ながい生活の後に、またながい悲しみの後に、またながい苦しみのその後の日に、あの安らかななつかしみと許しの日があるのだ。一日々々の苦しみや悲しみがなんだらう。一日々々の疲れやなやみがなんだらう。彼女はいつとなしに微笑を浮べてゐた。
curious.label: house-checked

notes.body: That day stays vague in the Japanese, not heaven or a better future; rest here is quiet peace, not the night-like eternal rest named elsewhere.
notes.span: There is {t:that-day} when everything changes into nostalgia and forgiveness and {t:rest}.

curious.en: [grouped with p24, p25] "Yes," the man said too, lifting his eyes. "It is only three years, isn't it. And yet we have been through a lot of troubles."

And at the same moment the child gave a great cry, and looking at her mother's face, "Umma-umma-umma-umma," banged the spoon down on the table.

curious.en: The young father hurriedly put cooked rice [gohan] into the child's mouth.
curious.ja: 父親は、あわてゝ子供の口に御飯を入れてやった。

curious.en: They at last laid down their chopsticks.
curious.ja: 彼等は、やがて箸をおいた。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "Just a little while longer." The man said it strongly, as if to himself.
curious.ja: 『もう少しの間だ。』男は強く独言のやうに云った。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "Yes, let us work, shall we." She said it calmly, with rest [ansoku] / peace [yasurakasa]. And holding the child on her lap, she put out her small nipple and began to nurse.
curious.ja: 『さうね、私たちは働きませうね。』彼女は、おちついて安らかに云った。そして子供を膝の上に抱きながら、小さな乳首をだして乳をのませ初めた。
curious.label: house-checked

notes.body: Rest here is yasurakasa, a quiet peacefulness, not the night-like ansoku rest of the vision in p17. The English keeps the two words distinct.

curious.en: "Come, let us clear up. And let us sleep; tomorrow let us get up early, shall we?"
curious.ja: 『さ、あとを片づけよう。そして寝よう、明日は早く起きようぢゃないか。』
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: At last the man stood up. And as he was about to begin clearing the table, the child had already closed her eyes with her cheek against the breast. All around had fallen quiet.
curious.ja: やがて、男は立ち上った。そしてテーブルを片づけ初めようとした時、もはや子供は乳房に頬をつけて眼を閉ぢてゐた。あたりは静まりかへった。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "It's a storm [aramashi — arashi]." The man stopped still and whispered.
curious.ja: 『嵐だな。』男は、立ちどまってさゝやいた。
curious.label: house-checked

notes.body: The same bare word, storm (arashi), opened the story and returned quietly inside her vision; the husband now whispers it again after the child sleeps. Nothing is solved.

student.en: Outside the now-dark door, a violent sound of rain and wind — a arashi — storm.
student.ja: いつか暗くなった戸の外に、激しい雨風の音がする、嵐だ。
student.label: house-checked

notes.body: Arashi is simply storm — rain and wind outside the door. The same bare word returns later in the evening.

student.en: The father and mother and child had gathered at the taku [teeburu] — low dining table under dentō — early domestic electric lamp hanging against the wall of the narrow room, about to have supper. Father and mother were both still really young. And the child was a chubby, round baby girl, just able to stand holding on to the taku [teeburu] — low dining table.
student.ja: 親子は、狭い部屋の壁際にぶらさがった、暗い電燈の下の卓に集まって、今夜食をしようとしてゐた。まだ本当に父も母も若かった。そして子供は漸く卓につかまって、立ってる事が出来る程の、くり〳〵と肥ってる女の子だった。
student.label: house-checked

notes.body: Table renders 卓 marked with ruby テーブル to mean a low dining table, and dark electric light is a single dim early domestic bulb hung against the wall.
notes.span: at the {t:table} under {t:electric-light} hanging against the wall of the narrow room

student.en: Neither the man nor the woman had yet a single wrinkle in the face. But in the shade of his thick eyebrows his hollowed, kind-looking eyes showed a weary colour of tiredness. And in her dark hair and about her slight shoulders could be seen a still deeper, sunken tiredness, and a drowsy peace.
student.ja: 男も女も、その顔にはまだ少しの皺もよってなかった。しかし男の濃い眉毛の陰のくぼんだ優しさうな瞳には、だるさうな疲れの色が見えてゐた。そして女の濃い髪のいろや、細やかな肩のあたりには、なほ打沈んだやうな深い疲れと、まどろむやうな安らかさとが見えてゐた。
student.label: house-checked

notes.body: A drowsy peace renders まどろむやうな安らかさ, the first sounding of the book's recurring peace/rest chord that later hardens into doctrine.
sources: p3 まどろむやうな安らかさ

student.en: The day had ended. The grief and suffering of that day were about to flow into the peace of night. And they smiled in silence, fixing their eyes on everything in the child.
student.ja: 一日が終ったのであった。その日の悲しみも苦しみも、夜の安らかさに流れやうとしてゐるのだった。そして、彼等は黙って微笑しながら、その子供のすべてに瞳を注いだ。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: Standing unsteadily, the child with fat, round, ball-like short hands tried without a moment's pause, and far too fast, to rake everything on the taku [teeburu] — low dining table about. So, smiling, they put all the rice bowls and the teapot and the aluminum pots and the rest under the taku [teeburu] — low dining table. On top of the taku [teeburu] — low dining table there was left only the small spoon the child held and a single small plate.
student.ja: 子供は、あぶなさうに立ちながら、肥えてまるく鞠のやうに短い両手で、すこしのすきまもなく、そしてあまりに早くテーブルの上のものを掻き廻さうとしてゐた。それで彼等は微笑みみながら、すべて茶碗や土瓶、アルミ鍋などを、テーブルの下に置いた。テーブルの上には、わづか子供の持つ小さなスプーンと小皿が一枚残されたばかりであった。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: But the child gave a noisy cry, full of small joy, and banged the spoon and the plate down on the taku [teeburu] — low dining table.
student.ja: けれども子供は、さわがしい、小さなよろこびに満ちた叫声を上げて、スプーンと皿をテーブルの上にたゝきつけた。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "You won't listen, will you." The young father gazed at the small round arms and at the child's eyes with long, dark lashes, moving nimbly, cleverly, without a pause, as if wondering what was to be done, and then with a smile over his whole face, pinching the child's round sticking-out cheek with his finger, he felt under the taku [teeburu] — low dining table for a big bowl as if searching and put it in the child's hand.
student.ja: 『きかない奴だな。』若い父親は、その小さなまるい腕や、敏捷に怜悧にすきもなく動いてる、黒みがちの睫のながい子供の瞳をぢっと見てゐると、どうしたらいゝだらうといふやうに、やがて顔一ぱいな微笑を持って、子供のまるくつき出た頬を指で一寸つまみながら、大きな茶碗をテーブルの下から探すやうにしてとると、彼女の手に渡した。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: She dished up the hot, fresh gohan — cooked rice / meal, with white steam rising thick, from the pot and handed it to him. And her young big eyes too, full of a motherly gladness, gazed at the never for a moment still, lovely small-bird ways of the child. And as if she could not bear it, muttering to herself, 'Whatever is to be done with this child,' as if the child were dear beyond all managing, she said firmly, "bōya — lit. little boy; fond generic address for a baby," but a smile overflowed from her face, and she looked at the man's face as if asking for help. And the three, as if they had forgotten everything, smiled at each other over the child, as if wondering what to do for the child. And for the child, they set about the meal with a warm bustle, and with a smile and gladness welling up of itself on top of it. And with the clattering noise, they did not hear the sound of rain and wind.
student.ja: 彼女は鍋から熱い炊き立ての、白い湯気が一ぱい立ち上ってる御飯をついで彼に渡した。そして彼女の若い大きな瞳も、母親らしい嬉しさにみちて子供の瞬間もぢっとしてない、小鳥のやうに愛らしい様子を見つめた。そして、たまらなささうに、この子はどうしたといふんだらう、とふと口の中に独言を云ひながら、どうにも仕方がない程可愛いといふやうな様子で、『坊や、』と強く云ったけれども、笑が顔からあふれて了って、彼女は助をかりるやうに男の顔を見た。そして三人は、すべての事を忘れてしまった様に、子供の為めに互にどうしようかといふ様に笑ひ合った。そして子供の為めに、彼等は暖かい賑かさと、其上に自然に溢れる笑ひと嬉しさを持って食事にとりかゝったのであった。また彼等は、ごた〳〵した騒がしさの為に、雨風の音を耳にしない。

And his eyes holding back the smile that welled up helplessly from the child, he held the child up and put a little food into that small red mouth. In the gaps, hastily opening his big mouth, he crammed gohan — cooked rice / meal into his own mouth.
student.ja: 若い父親は、彼の赤く大きな片手を忙しくテーブルの上に拡げてゐた。そしてその眼は子供によって仕方がなく湧き出た笑を堪へながら、子供をさゝへて、その小さな赤い口に僅の食物を入れてやった。そのすきに彼は、あわたゞしく大きな口を開けた、彼は彼自身の口のなかに御飯を押し込んだ。

student.en: The mother, leaning against the wall, bowed and silent, heaped onto a white plate the beef and onion, the carrot and jagaimo — potato; nimono-style stew simmered in the deep blue pot. And about to say something, she put a jagaimo — potato; nimono-style stew simmered sweet and soft into her mouth and looked at the man's face, but as if noticing something, she suddenly shut her mouth and gazed blankly at a far place.
student.ja: 母親は、壁によって黙ってうつむきながら藍色の深い鍋に煮た牛肉と玉葱と、人参とジャガ芋とを白い皿に盛ってゐた。そしてなにか云はうとして、甘く柔かく煮たジャガ芋を口のなかに入れて、男の顔を見たが、彼女はなにかに気がついたやうに、ふと口を閉ぢて茫然と遠い所を見た。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: The jagaimo — potato; nimono-style stew in her mouth was hard as if frozen, gritty and crunching, and very bad-tasting. Silently, as if startled, she re-bit it with her front teeth, but her heart had already bowed down, lonely.
student.ja: 彼女の口のなかのジャガ芋が、丁度凍ったかのやうに固くざく〳〵してゐて、非常に不味かったのだった。彼女はふと驚いたやうに黙って前歯でかみなほしたが、彼女の心は、いつか淋しくうつむいてしまってゐた。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: She had remembered the suffering and grief and tiredness of each day. And the tasteless, unrelated, cold badness of the jagaimo — potato; nimono-style stew gave her a quiet, lonely, far-away heart. She pictured the poor, grief-filled real life after marriage.
student.ja: 彼女は日々の苦しみや悲しみ疲れを思出したのであった。そしてジャガ芋の無味な、かゝはりのない冷やかな不味さが、彼女に静かな淋しい遠くはなれた心を与へた。彼女は結婚後の貧しい悲しみにみちた現実の生活を思ひ浮べたのであった。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: And it seemed like a life dragged on far too long. She felt suddenly as if she herself had grown quite old. And quietly, with a far heart, she was quietly remembering the tear-filled days, and the days spent threatened and afraid over material things, and the days, day by day, grieved and suffered through illness. But to her remembering now, everything was like a dream. Suffering too, grief too, were like a nostalgic dream.
student.ja: そして、それがあまりに永く引きつゞいた生活のやうにも思はれた。彼女はふと自分がすっかり老いてしまったかのやうに考へられた。そして静かに涙にみちた日のことや、物質の為めに脅かされ恐れてすごした日々や、病の為めに悲しみ苦しんだその日その日のことを遠い心が静かに思出してゐるのだった。けれどもいま思出してる彼女には、すべてが夢のやうであった。苦しみも悲しみもなつかしい夢のやうであった。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: And when you think about it, it was only about three years of life since marriage.
student.ja: そして考へて見れば、わづかに結婚後の三年ばかりの生活にすぎない。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: Before she knew it, as if caught by something, she gazed blankly toward the far distance. Her quiet heart was already seeing something like a phantom picture.
student.ja: 彼女は、いつとなく何物にか気をとられたやうに、ぼんやりと遠くの方を見てゐた。彼女のその静かな心が、いつか幻のやうな絵を見てゐたのであった。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: It was in a dim light, and, quiet like that light, three people drawing close with heads together, telling a long story. The story seemed to go on and on between them, for so long without ever breaking off. And in that story, all the good and evil of the world, sadness and suffering and anger and anguish and joy, everything seemed to be told. But teller and listener only quietly, peacefully, went on smiling, and they did not move at all. With heads bent and eyes lowered, only a quiet nostalgia and forgiveness seemed to wrap them there. And there too a deep, deep peace showed over all of them.
student.ja: それは淡暗い光りのなかに、そしてその光りのやうに物静かな三人の人たちが、より合って頭をあつめてながい物語りをしてゐるのだった。その物語りは、あまりにながく絶えることなく彼等の間につゞけられてゐるやうであった。そしてその物語りのなかには、すべて世の中の善や悪や、かなしみや苦しみ怒りもなやみも、よろこびもすべてが語られてるやうだった。けれども話す人も聞く人も、たゞ静かに安らかにぢっと微笑をつゞけてゐるばかりであって、彼等は少しも動かなかった。首をかたむけて眼を伏せながら、そして、そこにはたゞ静かななつかしみと、許しとが彼等をつつんでゐるやうに見えた。そしてまたそこには深い〳〵安らかさが彼等のすべてに表はれてゐるのであった。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: All the things of the world, a life, will pass. And on ano hi / sono hi — that day when it has passed, everything, all things, will for the first time change into nostalgia and forgiveness. And at ano hi / sono hi — that day they are before an eternal ansoku — rest/repose; yasurakasa — peacefulness like night.
student.ja: 世の中の總ての事、人生は過去るであらう。そして過去った其日に初めて總てが、總ての事が懐しみと許しとに変る事だらう。そして其時彼等は永久に夜の様な安息の前にあるのであった。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: The far picture was reflected dark and quiet in the bottom of her eyes. And through the bottom of her eyes, far off into the future, with a lonely peace, that picture could be seen. Young, alone, she gave a lonely secret sigh, and, glancing at the scattered taku [teeburu] — low dining table and the faces of her husband and child, she stayed silent.
student.ja: 遠い絵が暗く静かに、彼女の眼の底に映ってゐた。また瞳の底を通して遠く未来に、淋しい安らかさを持って、その絵が見えるのであった。若い彼女は一人で淋しいひそかな溜息をついた、そして、とり散らされたテーブルの上と、夫と子供の顔をちらと見ながら黙ってゐた。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "Why are you so quiet?" The man looked at the woman's face in sudden wonder and spoke to her. She hurried to say something, but unable to say it all at once she fell silent, and again her eyes ran far away. And she saw the phantom picture again. Then for the first time she quietly heard the sound of the arashi — storm outside the door. She said nothing.
student.ja: 『どうして黙ってるの。』男は、ふと不思議さうに女の顔を見て声をかけた。彼女は、あわてゝなにかを云はうとしたが、一口には何事も云ひかねて黙ってしまふと、再びその眼が遠く走ってしまった。そして彼女は、また幻の絵を見たのだった。彼女は、その時はじめて戸の外の嵐の音を、静かに耳にした。彼女はなにも云はずにゐた。
student.label: house-checked

notes.body: The storm opened the story and was then forgotten in the table noise; here she hears it again, quietly, from inside her distance.
notes.span: Then for the first time she quietly heard the sound of the {t:storm} outside the door.

student.en: Yes. There is ano hi / sono hi — that day. There is ano hi / sono hi — that day when everything changes into nostalgia and forgiveness and ansoku — rest/repose; yasurakasa — peacefulness. After a long life, and after a long grief, and after a long suffering, on the day after that, there is that peaceful ano hi / sono hi — that day of nostalgia and forgiveness. What is the suffering and grief of each single day. What is the tiredness and worry of each single day. Before she knew it she was smiling a smile.
student.ja: さうだ。あの日があるのだ。あのすべてがなつかしみと許しと、安らかさに変る日があるのだった。ながい生活の後に、またながい悲しみの後に、またながい苦しみのその後の日に、あの安らかななつかしみと許しの日があるのだ。一日々々の苦しみや悲しみがなんだらう。一日々々の疲れやなやみがなんだらう。彼女はいつとなしに微笑を浮べてゐた。
student.label: house-checked

notes.body: That day stays vague in the Japanese, not heaven or a better future; rest here is quiet peace, not the night-like eternal rest named elsewhere.
notes.span: There is {t:that-day} when everything changes into nostalgia and forgiveness and {t:rest}.

student.ja: 『なぜ黙ってるの。』男は再び声をかけた。彼女は驚いたやうに頭を上げて、なつかしさうに笑ひながら、

student.ja: 『まだ本当にわづかしか経ちませんのね、結婚してから。』

student.en: She said it as if asking him too to remember, and all sorts of things, even the happy things from before they married, to remember.
student.ja: と男にも思出して、種々のことを、結婚前の楽しかったことまでも、思出して下さいと云ふやうに云った。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: [grouped with p24, p25] "Yes," the man said too, lifting his eyes. "It is only three years, isn't it. And yet we have been through a lot of troubles."
student.ja: 『さうだなァ。』男も眼を上げて云った。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "Yes," the man said too, lifting his eyes. "It is only three years, isn't it. And yet we have been through all sorts of troubles."
student.ja: 『たった三年にしかならないんだな。けれども、俺たちはいろ〳〵苦労したなァ。』

student.en: [grouped with p26, p27] "Quite true." She lowered her eyes again to try to see that picture. But at once, "But still only three years have passed, haven't they," she said, her eyes shining as if she had to tell him some great hope, though she did not herself know what great thing it was.
student.ja: 『本当にね。』彼女は、また眼を伏せてあの絵を見ようとした。が、すぐに、
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "Quite true." She lowered her eyes again to try to see that picture. But at once, "But still only three years have passed, haven't they," she said, her eyes shining as if she had to tell him some great hope, though she did not herself know what great hope it was.
student.ja: 『けれども、まだ三年しか経たないんですものね。』と、なにか大きな、彼女にはわからないけれども、なにか大きな希みを彼に話さなければならないやうに瞳を輝かした。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "That's right. Even though day by day we are tired out and troubled and made to suffer by one thing and another, two years are already past. In a little while bōya — lit. little boy; fond generic address for a baby will be walking too."
student.ja: 『さうだ、一日々々いろ〳〵なことに疲らされなやまされ苦しまされても、二年はもう過ぎたんだからな。もうしばらくすると、坊やも歩るくやうになるんだから。』
student.label: house-checked

notes.body: The Japanese says two years are already past here, though the marriage is counted as three years elsewhere; the draft keeps the inconsistency literal.

student.en: The young father hurriedly put gohan — cooked rice / meal into the child's mouth.
student.ja: 父親は、あわてゝ子供の口に御飯を入れてやった。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: They at last laid down their chopsticks.
student.ja: 彼等は、やがて箸をおいた。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "Just a little while longer." The man said it strongly, as if to himself.
student.ja: 『もう少しの間だ。』男は強く独言のやうに云った。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "Yes, let us work, shall we." She said it calmly, with ansoku — rest/repose; yasurakasa — peacefulness. And holding the child on her lap, she put out her small nipple and began to nurse.
student.ja: 『さうね、私たちは働きませうね。』彼女は、おちついて安らかに云った。そして子供を膝の上に抱きながら、小さな乳首をだして乳をのませ初めた。
student.label: house-checked

notes.body: Rest here is yasurakasa, a quiet peacefulness, not the night-like ansoku rest of the vision in p17. The English keeps the two words distinct.

student.en: "Come, let us clear up. And let us sleep; tomorrow let us get up early, shall we?"
student.ja: 『さ、あとを片づけよう。そして寝よう、明日は早く起きようぢゃないか。』
student.label: house-checked

student.en: At last the man stood up. And as he was about to begin clearing the taku [teeburu] — low dining table, the child had already closed her eyes with her cheek against the breast. All around had fallen quiet.
student.ja: やがて、男は立ち上った。そしてテーブルを片づけ初めようとした時、もはや子供は乳房に頬をつけて眼を閉ぢてゐた。あたりは静まりかへった。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "It's a arashi — storm." The man stopped still and whispered.
student.ja: 『嵐だな。』男は、立ちどまってさゝやいた。
student.label: house-checked

notes.body: The same bare word, storm (arashi), opened the story and returned quietly inside her vision; the husband now whispers it again after the child sleeps. Nothing is solved.
